title: Firmware & Electronics Engineer, Wearables
description: About the job Wualt is building a smart ring for women's safety and everyday wellness. The ring senses what the body is doing and, when it matters, alerts the people a wearer trusts. We are a funded, pre-launch hardware startup heading into our first field pilots in early 2027 and launch in mid 2027. Small team, real hardware, real users, close to the founders. The role The firmware and electronics are what make the ring a product and not a prototype. We are looking for one person to own that layer end to end: the firmware on the ring, the board and its electronics, bring-up, and the path from a bench board to a device on a real finger. You would own the ring firmware and the electronics design, including schematic capture and PCB layout, and validate the hardware together with our Head of Product and our manufacturing vendor. We need a go-getter who can carry this part of the product largely on their own. Experience we expect (please read before applying) • Around 4 years (3 to 5) writing production embedded firmware in C or C++ for battery-powered devices. Wearable or small-form-factor IoT experience matters far more than total years. • Hands-on with ARM Cortex-M class microcontrollers and low-power wireless (BLE). Experience with low-power wireless SoCs is a strong plus. • You design the hardware too: schematic capture and PCB layout (Altium, KiCad or similar). You are well versed in taking a board from schematic to a working, manufacturable design, not just reading one. • Real BLE experience: GATT services, low-power connection management, bonding, and reconnection. Experience with OTA or DFU firmware updates is preferred. • Sensor integration over I2C and SPI at the register level: optical or PPG sensors, IMU or accelerometer, power sequencing, and clean sampling. • Ultra-low-power design and debugging: sleep states, power budgeting on a coin or Li-po battery, and comfort with an oscilloscope, logic analyzer, and multimeter. What we expect you to do • Own the ring firmware end to end and be accountable for a pilot-ready device. Our first field pilots start early 2027, and launch follows mid 2027. • Own the electronics: schematic capture and PCB layout for a ring-scale, space and power constrained form factor, and validate every board with the Head of Product and the manufacturing vendor. You will lay out the flex PCB and review fit and manufacturability with the mechanical and manufacturing partners before fabrication. • Bring up boards, write and maintain the drivers for the device's optical and motion sensors, and own the BLE link, power path, and charging behaviour. Integrate microphone capture and verify that audio reaches the phone alongside sensor data. • Protect signal quality at the source: deliver clean, well-timed raw sensor data that the ML and algorithms team can actually trust. • Own the firmware and electronics side of design-for-manufacture, test fixtures, and production bring-up, working with the mechanical and manufacturing vendors. • Hold the bar on reliability, power, and field behaviour, and say no to anything that will not survive a real wearer. • Measure current draw during sleep, sensor sampling and BLE transfers. Compare measured runtime against the power budget and verify charging through the ring's contacts. • Test BLE stability and reconnection with the assembled ring worn on the finger, across ring sizes and phone positions. Work with the antenna partner to diagnose weak or intermittent links. • Verify end-to-end behaviour with the mobile team: test what the wearer experiences when the battery is low, the ring restarts, or the phone disconnects and reconnects. Bonus • Wearables, health-tech, medical-device, or femtech hardware experience. • Flex or rigid-flex PCB design and small-form-factor or high-density layout. Hands-on flex layout experience is especially valuable for this role. • Battery and charging design, including wireless or inductive charging. For this ring, experience with small rechargeable cells, charger or PMIC integration, and contact-based charging is especially relevant. • Analog front-end design for biosignals. • Experience with Nordic's nRF Connect SDK, Zephyr or FreeRTOS. • Experience taking a device through certification, DFM, and a first production run. • A personal hardware project that shows you cannot stop building things. What you get • Full ownership of the firmware and electronics at a company that is weeks, not years, from putting its product on real people. • Hardware you can hold, a pilot on a real timeline, and a direct line to the founders. • Competitive salary. To apply, tell us about a battery-powered BLE device you helped take from schematic to working hardware: which parts of the circuit and firmware you personally owned, what you measured to diagnose a problem during bring-up, and how you verified the fix.
